question: A 3-day-old neonate born by normal vaginal delivery develops fever, bulging anterior fontanelle, and poor feeding. Which organism is the most likely cause of meningitis in this patient?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Group B Streptococcus is the most common cause of neonatal meningitis, acquired from the maternal genital tract during vaginal delivery. Other important neonatal pathogens include E. coli (K1 capsule) and Listeria monocytogenes.

N. meningitidis is the most common cause of meningitis in older children and young adults (3 months to 18 years) in India, not in the neonatal period. Neonates lack the nasopharyngeal colonisation that precedes meningococcal disease.
Pneumococcal meningitis becomes important after 3 months of age and is the most common cause in adults aged 18–50 years. It is uncommon in the first week of life.
H. influenzae type b was historically important in children aged 3 months to 5 years, especially before widespread Hib vaccination. It is not a typical neonatal pathogen.

overallFeedback.feedback: Revisit the age–organism table. In neonates (<4 weeks), the most common organisms are Group B Streptococcus, E. coli (K1 capsule), and Listeria monocytogenes — all acquired from the maternal genital tract during delivery.

The neonatal meningitis triad — Group B Streptococcus, E. coli K1, and Listeria — reflects organisms acquired from the maternal genital tract and birth canal. Knowing the age–organism correlation is essential for choosing empiric antibiotics.
